description:
We are the PiGênios! Our team is made up of a family of three brothers, with infinite ideas and a mission focused on the future of food for our planet.

We are passionate about astronomy and technology. We chose the challenge “Farming for the Future: Adapting Farms with NASA Data” because we want to put our skills and creativity to work for the world.

“One small step for children, one giant leap for humanity!”
summary:
The project is based on a real-world problem. On November 4, 2026, a tornado devastated crops in Chapecó, causing more than R$13 million in agricultural losses.

In the face of this event, we asked ourselves: how can we continue producing food when the climate is becoming increasingly unpredictable? Irregular rainfall, temperature changes, excess or scarcity of water, and their impacts represent growing challenges for agriculture.

With this in mind, we created **AgroAlertSC**, a territorial intelligence application that uses data from NASA satellites and Earth observation systems to transform scientific information into risk alerts and practical guidance for farmers.
The platform aims to support planting decisions, climate adaptation, crop rotation, and soil conservation, helping farmers anticipate threats and reduce potential losses.
Our goal is to bring space science closer to the realities of farming, contributing to a more resilient, sustainable agriculture that is better prepared for the climate challenges of the future.
**Because protecting food production today means protecting everyone's future.**
details:
AgroAlert SC – Infinite Ideas to Save the Harvest

Our project was born from a major challenge: helping agriculture face the effects of climate change and natural disasters.

Our initial focus was the city of Chapecó, in Santa Catarina, Brazil, which was completely destroyed by the events of November 4, 2026. Faced with this reality, we understood that rebuilding does not simply mean recovering what was lost, but also finding new ways of doing things. It means reinventing ourselves.

We draw an analogy with the ideas of Domenico De Masi, who believed that creativity emerges when dreams are combined with action. Countries that are now global references in innovation have also experienced periods of destruction and reconstruction. It was precisely through overcoming difficulties that they discovered new opportunities to innovate.

What does our project do, and how does it work?

We created AgroAlert SC, an application that uses NASA satellite data to monitor environmental conditions and identify potential threats to crops. Its purpose is to provide farmers with early warnings, allowing them to make informed decisions before damage occurs.

But our project goes beyond prevention. We created a special feature called "Start Again."

Imagine a farmer who has lost their entire crop in a flood. Instead of simply receiving an alert about the disaster, they can access suggestions for alternative crops, especially short-cycle varieties that can be replanted and harvested in less time. This gives farmers an opportunity to recover part of their production, generate income again, and rebuild their agricultural activities.

What benefits and impacts do we aim to achieve?

Our main goal is to protect agricultural production, reduce financial losses, strengthen food security, and provide alternatives for farmers facing extreme situations.

We want technology to become a tool for prevention, recovery, and hope. We do not just want to help farmers save their next harvest; we also want to show that even after losing everything, it is possible to start again.

What makes our project creative?

The greatest innovation of AgroAlert SC is its ability to combine prevention and reconstruction in a single solution. While many tools focus on identifying risks, our application also considers what happens after a disaster.

The "Start Again" feature represents this vision: transforming data, technology, and creativity into real opportunities for those whose livelihoods depend on agriculture.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project is based on Earth observation data provided by NASA, with the goal of integrating this information into an application for agricultural monitoring and guidance.
